item.text: The continuation search found usable target-period material for election administration, online voting, observer restrictions, protest surveillance, leader-centered ideology, and political equality. It also confirmed that succession evidence remains mostly structural rather than an actual 2022 transfer event; I’ll preserve that as an unresolved gap rather than treating absence as evidence of conduct.

Review round 1 continuation completed for Chapter 4B, lenses 4B.1–4B.10. No score assigned.

The workspace remained read-only, so I could not update `research-materials.md` or `research-ledger-manifest.json`. The new ledger entries below are the authoritative continuation handoff and use globally new IDs E017–E025.

New accepted evidence:

- E017 — OSW, “Russia: regional (pseudo)elections in the shadow of war,” 15 September 2022, lines 48–50. Russia held gubernatorial, regional-parliamentary, city-council, and municipal elections on 11 September; official results showed pro-Kremlin candidates winning, while Navalny-linked “Smart Vote” had no success. Maps 4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.8. [OSW](https://www.osw.waw.pl/en/publikacje/analyses/2022-09-15/russia-regional-pseudo-elections-shadow-war)

- E018 — Same source, lines 52–56. Incumbent or United Russia-backed governors won; United Russia and the mayor-backed My District movement won over 90% of Moscow municipal seats; Golos reported the lowest regional-parliament competitiveness indicator since 2012. Maps 4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.3, 4B.10. Attribution is system-level and mediated through regional authorities, not proof of Putin’s personal intervention.

- E019 — Same source, lines 57–60. Independent campaigns were described as highly risky; candidates were excluded through politically motivated convictions or “fake news” and “discrediting the army” cases; multi-day and online voting reduced observer scrutiny and enabled possible result correction. Maps 4B.2, 4B.3, 4B.4, 4B.6, 4B.8, 4B.9.

- E020 — Same source, lines 61–64. The Kremlin sought to display wartime consensus, marginalize elections in state media, and prevent unexpected outcomes; OSW characterizes the elections as politically insignificant spectacles. This is an analytic source claim, not a verified personal order. Maps 4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.5, 4B.10.

- E021 — EPDE, “No international politically-biased observers identified during the 2022 Russian regional elections,” lines 84–100. CEC chair Ella Pamfilova said international observers were not provided for by the applicable legal framework; EPDE reports that Russian authorities adhered to a restrictive interpretation excluding international observation. Maps 4B.2, 4B.4, 4B.6, 4B.10. [EPDE](https://epde.org/?news=no-international-politically-biased-observers-identified-during-the-2022-russian-regional-elections)

- E022 — U.S. Department of State, 2022 Russia Human Rights Report, lines 43 and 202. The report records inability to change government through free and fair elections, restrictions on opposition candidates and campaign activity, limits on civil-society election monitoring, media suppression, and severe assembly/association restrictions. It separately records serious abuses in occupied areas, which must not be generalized automatically to the Russian Federation. Maps 4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.3, 4B.7, 4B.10. [Report](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089062.html)

- E023 — OVD-Info, “Repressions in Russia in 2022,” Russian-language page, lines 67–81. OVD-Info reports more than 21,000 detentions, at least 370 criminal-case subjects for anti-war speech or activity, more than 200,000 blocked internet resources, 19,478 anti-war detentions from 24 February, facial-recognition detentions in Moscow Metro, and repeated police violence. Maps 4B.3, 4B.5, 4B.6, 4B.9, 4B.10. Counts are monitor-generated and should not be treated as complete national denominators. [ОВД-Инфо](https://data.ovd.info/repressii-v-rossii-v-2022-godu)

- E024 — OVD-Info, same page, lines 76–87. The 2022 record included environmental, labor-rights, anti-corruption, LGBT-related, Navalny-support, and anti-war actions; women comprised approximately 45% of identified anti-war detainees, rising to 51% and 71% in the 21 and 24 September mobilization protests. Maps 4B.3 and 4B.7. This provides evidence of political participation and gendered exposure to repression, not a complete measure of women’s political equality.

- E025 — Carnegie Endowment, “Scientific Putinism: Shaping Official Ideology in Russia,” 21 November 2022, lines 74–88. The article describes a presidentially initiated “Fundamentals of Russian Statehood” curriculum, official ideological unification, the labeling of dissenters as “fifth column,” “foreign agents,” or traitors, and a 2022 war narrative centered on Putinism and leader-sacrifice. Maps 4B.5, 4B.6, 4B.7, 4B.10. Attribution is stronger than for generic propaganda because the source identifies presidential initiatives, but the article is interpretive and should not be treated as proof of a formal personality-cult decree. [Carnegie Endowment](https://carnegieendowment.org/russia-eurasia/politika/2022/11/scientific-putinism-shaping-official-ideology-in-russia)

Authority baseline correction:

- E002 should be retained as the stable reusable authority item, with explicit mappings to 4B.1–4B.10. Article 80 establishes the president’s formal responsibility for internal and foreign-policy guidelines and constitutional rights.
- E001 remains context only and gateway-only; it should be excluded from the defensible evidence count.

Gap resolution:

- 4B.1 and 4B.2: materially strengthened with direct 11 September 2022 regional-election evidence, including competitiveness, candidate exclusion, online voting, and observer restrictions.
- 4B.4: partially improved through evidence that electoral and judicial mechanisms operated under executive/systemic pressure. No clear 2022 example was found of Putin accepting a binding institutional constraint.
- 4B.5: improved through E025’s leader-centered ideological curriculum and E018–E020’s Kremlin-centered electoral management. Direct evidence of a formal personality-cult institution remains limited.
- 4B.7: improved for women’s exposure to protest repression and for unequal treatment of minority/LGBTQ+ groups through the State Department report, but target-year representation and electoral access data remain incomplete.
- 4B.8: not materially resolved. The 2022 period contained no presidential transfer or succession event. Reuters reported that Putin had not yet stated whether he would seek another term and that the next presidential election was scheduled for 2024; this is context, not evidence of a 2022 transfer decision. [Reuters via Euronews](https://www.euronews.com/2022/11/03/ukraine-crisis-putin)
- Leader-centered control: strengthened, but personal attribution remains bounded. Formal presidential authority, Putin’s signed censorship laws, his mobilization call, and presidential ideological initiatives support attribution for selected acts; generalized conduct by courts, police, election commissions, and regional authorities remains institutional rather than personally ordered.

Local-fact disposition audit:

- LF001, LF003–LF009, LF013–LF015: retained as structured country-year baseline/context.
- LF002 and LF010: retained as Freedom House political/civil-liberties context.
- LF011–LF012: retained as direct press-environment context.
- LF016–LF017: retained as governance/rule-of-law context.
- None were discarded; none establish personal ruler attribution without narrative corroboration.

The chapter is better covered after this bounded round, but not fully saturated on succession, direct institutional self-restraint, and target-year minority/women representation. No score or score range is provided.
